lower-0862-s8-test-a-pattern.description: Compare repeating changes and explain when a claim fails.

sections.title: What changes each time?
sections.label: Growth and start
sections.intro: Separate the part that grows with the row number from the part that stays fixed. To check whether a total can occur, remove the fixed part and see whether the rest makes a whole number of groups.

blocks.html: In a rule of the form \(an+b\), the coefficient \(a\) is the step between terms. The fixed part \(b\) accounts for the starting offset.

figure.alt: Rows with one, two and three blue triples followed by two amber tiles.
figure.caption: Each new row adds one blue triple. The two amber tiles stay fixed.

blocks.prompt:
Build row \(n\) with 5 tiles for each group and 4 extra tiles at the end. Row \(n\) has \(n\) groups.

Row number123
Tiles91419

How many tiles are in row 8?
blocks.hint: Row 8 contains eight groups of five. Add the four fixed tiles once.
blocks.solution:
Row 8 has 8 groups. Multiply 8 by 5 and add the 4 tiles at the end.

\(44\)

retry.feedback: The groups are correct. Include the fixed tiles at the end of the row.

blocks.html: The first term includes some growing tiles. Putting the entire first term into the fixed part would count those tiles twice.

blocks.title: Find the largest row that fits
blocks.prompt: Row \(n\) uses \(n\) groups of 4 tiles and 3 fixed tiles. You have 34 tiles. What is the largest row number you can build?
blocks.hint: Set aside the three fixed tiles, then count complete groups of four that fit.
blocks.solution: After setting aside 3 tiles, \(34-3=31\) tiles remain. Seven groups need 28, while eight need 32. The largest row number is 7.

retry.feedback: Eight groups would need 32 tiles plus the three fixed tiles. Only 34 tiles are available.

blocks.prompt:
Build row \(n\) with 6 tiles for each group and 4 extra tiles at the end. Row \(n\) has \(n\) groups.

Row number123
Tiles101622

How many tiles are in row 8?
blocks.hint: Here each group has six tiles. Only the group count changes from row to row.
blocks.solution:
Row 8 has 8 groups. Multiply 8 by 6 and add the 4 tiles at the end.

\(52\)

retry.feedback: The groups are correct. Include the fixed tiles at the end of the row.

blocks.html: Test a proposed rule by substituting more than one row number.

sections.title: Can the same fence cover a different area?
sections.label: One counterexample
sections.intro: A claim that says ‘always’ has to work in every allowed case. To test a claim about perimeter and area, keep the perimeter fixed and look for two designs with different products of their side lengths.

blocks.html: The fixed perimeter controls the sum of length and width. The area depends on their product, which can change even when the sum stays fixed.

figure.alt: An 8 by 2 rectangle and a 6 by 4 rectangle share the same outline length.
figure.caption: Both designs use a 20 m fence. The 4 m wide rectangle covers more ground.

blocks.prompt:
A gardener uses 72 metres of fencing around a rectangle. The first design has width 4 m. The second has width 6 m.

Find the length of the second rectangle in metres.
blocks.hint: Half of the 72 m perimeter is one length plus one width. Use the second design’s width of 6 m.
blocks.solution:
Length plus width is half the perimeter, which is 36 m. Subtract the new width 6 m.

\(30\) m

retry.feedback: The fence includes both lengths and both widths. Halve the perimeter before subtracting the width.

blocks.html: Use the correct length for each width. Keeping both the first length and the new width changes the fence needed.

blocks.title: Compare two areas inside the same fence
blocks.prompt: Two rectangles each use 28 m of fencing. One is 3 m wide and the other is 5 m wide. By how many square metres do their areas differ?
blocks.hint: Find the length of each rectangle from half its perimeter before finding the two areas.
blocks.solution: One length plus one width is \(28\div2=14\) m. The areas are \(3\times11=33\) and \(5\times9=45\) square metres. The difference is \(45-33=12\) square metres.

retry.feedback: The perimeters match. The areas use multiplication, so find each area separately.

blocks.prompt:
A gardener uses 74 metres of fencing around a rectangle. The first design has width 4 m. The second has width 6 m.

Find the length of the second rectangle in metres.
blocks.hint: The full perimeter includes two lengths and two widths. Halve 74 before taking away the second width.
blocks.solution:
Length plus width is half the perimeter, which is 37 m. Subtract the new width 6 m.

\(31\) m

retry.feedback: The fence includes both lengths and both widths. Halve the perimeter before subtracting the width.

blocks.html: To disprove an “always” claim, give one clear example that satisfies the conditions but gives a different result.

sections.title: Do two opposite changes cancel?
sections.label: Percent base
sections.intro: The amount after a percentage change becomes the starting amount for the next change. To undo a rise, find what fraction of the new amount must be removed. A fall by the same percentage uses a different base.

blocks.html: Each percentage acts on the current amount. The same percentage of the larger bar is a bigger quantity.

figure.alt: A bar for 100 grows to 120. Taking 20 per cent of 120 leaves 96.
figure.caption: The rise adds 20. The fall removes 24 because the reference amount is now 120.

blocks.prompt:
A machine setting is 550 units. It rises by 55% and then falls by 55%. Each percentage is taken from the current setting.

Find the final setting in units.
blocks.hint: After the 55% rise, keep the full new amount. The fall leaves 45% of that amount.
blocks.solution:
After the rise, multiply the starting value by \(\frac{31}{20}\) to get \(\frac{1705}{2}\).

The fall uses that new value. Multiply it by \(\frac{9}{20}\) to get \(\frac{3069}{8}\).

\(\frac{3069}{8}\) units

retry.feedback: The rise and fall use different starting amounts. Apply the second percentage to the new setting.

blocks.html: Taking both changes from the first amount makes them cancel in the calculation. The problem says the amount changes between steps.

blocks.title: Find a decrease from the new price
blocks.prompt: A shop increases the price of a bag from £40 to £50. What percentage decrease from £50 brings it back to £40?
blocks.hint: Find the amount removed, then compare it with the price just before the decrease.
blocks.solution: The amount removed is £10. The starting price for the decrease is £50, so the decrease is \(\frac{10}{50}\times100\%=20\%\).

retry.feedback: 25% compares the £10 with the original £40. The decrease starts at £50.

blocks.prompt:
A machine setting is 575 units. It rises by 55% and then falls by 55%. Each percentage is taken from the current setting.

Find the final setting in units.
blocks.hint: Apply the multiplier for the rise to 575 first. Apply the multiplier for the fall to that new result.
blocks.solution:
After the rise, multiply the starting value by \(\frac{31}{20}\) to get \(\frac{3565}{4}\).

The fall uses that new value. Multiply it by \(\frac{9}{20}\) to get \(\frac{6417}{16}\).

\(\frac{6417}{16}\) units

retry.feedback: The rise and fall use different starting amounts. Apply the second percentage to the new setting.

blocks.html: Write both multipliers and round only at the end if asked.

examples.title: A growing row of tiles
examples.question:
Build row \(n\) with 6 tiles for each group and one extra tile at the end. Row \(n\) has \(n\) groups.

Row number123
Tiles71319

  1. How many tiles are in row 7?

    [2]

  2. Write a rule for the number of tiles in row \(n\).

    [2]

  3. Which row uses 61 tiles?

    [2]
solution: (a) Row 7 has 7 groups. Multiply 7 by 6 and add the extra tile at the end.
(b) The groups contribute \(6n\). The extra tile stays the same.
(c) Take off the fixed tile to leave whole groups of size 6.

examples.title: Decide whether a total fits the pattern
examples.question: Each row has \(n\) groups of 5 tiles and 2 extra tiles, where \(n\) is a positive whole number. Can a row use exactly 47 tiles? Can it use exactly 49?
solution: Write the total as \(5n+2\). Take away the two fixed tiles before testing for groups of five.
For 47 tiles, \(47-2=45\). This makes 9 complete groups, so row 9 fits.
For 49 tiles, \(49-2=47=5\times9+2\). Two tiles are left after the nine groups, so 49 is not a row total.

examples.title: Rearranging a fixed fence
examples.question:
A gardener uses 70 metres of fencing around a rectangle. The first design has width 3 m. The second has width 5 m.

  1. Find the length of the second rectangle in metres.

    [2]

  2. Work out how much the area increases, in square metres.

    [2]

  3. Someone says that equal perimeters always give equal areas. Does this example support the claim? Explain.

    [2]
solution: (a) Length plus width is half the perimeter, which is 35 m. Subtract the new width 5 m.
(b) The first area is 3 times 32, giving 96. The second area is 5 times 30, giving 150.
Subtract 96 from 150.
\(54\) square metres
(c) The area changed by 54 square metres, even though the fence length stayed fixed.
No. The two perimeters are equal, but the areas differ.

examples.title: Use one comparison to disprove an area claim
examples.question: Mina claims all rectangles made with 24 m of fencing have the same area. Compare a 3 m wide rectangle with a 5 m wide rectangle. Does the claim hold?
solution: The widths and lengths must add to \(24\div2=12\) m. The lengths are \(12-3=9\) m and \(12-5=7\) m.
The two areas are \(3\times9=27\) and \(5\times7=35\) square metres.
Both rectangles have 24 m of fencing, and their areas differ. These two cases disprove the claim.

examples.title: Up, then down by the same percentage
examples.question:
A machine setting is 825 units. It rises by 40% and then falls by 40%. Each percentage is taken from the current setting.

  1. Find the final setting in units.

    [2]

  2. How many units smaller is the final setting than the original?

    [2]

  3. Explain why the rise and fall do not cancel.

    [2]
solution: (a) After the rise, multiply the starting value by \(\frac{7}{5}\) to get \(1155\).
The fall uses that new value. Multiply it by \(\frac{3}{5}\) to get \(693\).
(b) The original is 825. Take away \(693\) using exact values.
(c) Compare the first percentage of 825 with the second percentage of \(1155\).
The fall takes the same percentage of the larger amount, so it removes more units than the rise added.

examples.title: Find the percentage decrease that undoes a rise
examples.question: A bicycle helmet rises from £80 to £100. Find the percentage rise. What percentage decrease from £100 would return it to £80?
solution: The rise is £20 out of the original £80. The percentage rise is \(\frac{20}{80}\times100\%=25\%\).
The fall is also £20, but it starts at £100. The percentage decrease is \(\frac{20}{100}\times100\%=20\%\).
Both changes are £20. The first percentage is based on £80 and the second on £100.
